sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

content.text:
Case F18: segment the fibrous soft-tissue tumor on this T2-weighted MRI.

Volume: 281x281x235 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case F18 | sequence T2 | shape (i,j,k)=(281, 281, 235) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: fibrous soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).
axial 117/235 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 1/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking: The anatomy here is confusing me—the axial view looks unusual, like it's showing an abdomen with a large mass. I need to look at more of the image sheets to make sense of it.

sheet coronal 40–240/281 (12 slices) | v0 | tool calls 3/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm puzzled by the imaging orientation here—the axial slices seem to show spine, cord, and kidneys, but there's also a large homogeneous oval mass with vessels running through it that looks almost liver-like, and a similar structure appears in the coronal views too.

Tracking the two kidney-like structures through the axial and coronal slices, I'm trying to figure out whether that smooth-margined oval mass sitting below the kidney is actually the tumor, possibly a desmoid given the heterogeneous bright appearance near the anterior abdominal wall.

content.text: coronal 160/281 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 4/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm trying to figure out whether this large homogeneous oval mass near the kidney is actually liver tissue, given the branching vascular pattern resembling portal veins seen on the axial slices. The positioning is confusing though, since liver is normally superior to the kidney but this mass appears inferior to it on the coronal image.

I'm reconsidering the orientation entirely — the low axial slices showing a dark cavity surrounded by ribs suggest lung, meaning lower indices correspond to the chest and higher ones move toward the pelvis. Tracking through the axial slices sequentially, I'm trying to map the liver, heart, stomach, and kidney based on their expected position along that superior-to-inferior progression.

But the coronal slices complicate this: if kidney appears above the mass at the top of the image, that's inconsistent with liver normally sitting above kidney, unless the coronal display itself is flipped vertically. Looking at structures like the thecal sac tapering and fluffy bowel-like regions near the top with what looks like a thigh at the bottom, I'm now suspecting the coronal series may actually be displayed upside-down.

This scan is confusing me — the patient might be positioned obliquely. Rather than keep guessing between "liver" and "mass" from these conflicting coronal cues, I should check the sagittal images to clarify the anatomy.

content.text: sheet sagittal 60–220/281 (12 slices) | v0 | tool calls 5/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
Looking at this sagittal sheet, I realize the slices actually resemble coronal views, with the spine vertical and kidneys appearing on both sides. In slice 176, I can see the right kidney next to a large homogeneous structure resembling liver tissue lateral and inferior to it, while the left kidney appears on the right side of the image.

I also notice a bright, heterogeneous region along the anterior abdominal wall across several slices, with lobulated, fluffy signal that could suggest something like a desmoid rather than normal bowel. Checking axial slice 111, I spot branching vessels converging centrally, which is characteristic of hepatic veins meeting the IVC, confirming that structure as liver rather than tumor. This suggests the actual lesion is more likely that anterior abdominal wall abnormality I noted, which I want to examine further on axial 147.

content.text: axial 150/235 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 6/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm trying to localize the kidney relative to the oval structure anterior to it, which looks homogeneous and similarly intense — possibly the mass itself. The branching vessels nearby suggest liver tissue, and this anterior oval seems to track down into the larger oval mass seen on the coronal view.

There's also a huge dark homogeneous region occupying much of the left abdomen that could be a fibrous tumor like a desmoid given its low signal, though it might just be an oddly large psoas or paraspinal muscle given the tilted, oblique imaging plane. The body's asymmetric compression on the right makes orientation tricky, so I'm trying to decide whether this smooth-edged dark region is pathological or just distorted normal anatomy.

content.text: sagittal 118/281 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 7/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
The sagittal slices look blurry because the volume was resampled from thick slices, while the in-plane acquisition was axial and sharp—so axial must be the true acquisition plane. Looking back at axial slice 150, I'm trying to sort out the anatomy: there's a kidney with renal pelvis near 1775, a vertebral body with cord around 1762, and what might be a second structure posterior to the spine near 1685 that I need to identify.

Kidneys shouldn't sit posterior to the spine, so something's off—maybe this isn't a straightforward axial image, or the patient has severe scoliosis causing an oblique cut that makes one kidney appear in an unusual position. I'm also reconsidering whether the bright ring at 1762 is actually a vertebra with CSF around a dark cord on fat-sat T2, and whether the sagittal slices might actually be displaying coronal-style anatomy with kidneys appearing on either side of a vertical spine.

Looking more carefully at kidney orientation in the sagittal images, I notice the upper pole should normally tilt medially while the lower pole is more lateral—but in these images that relationship seems reversed, suggesting the display might simply be flipped upside-down, with "top" actually representing the inferior direction. That would mean the large homogeneous structure I thought was below the kidney is actually positioned where the liver should be, superior-lateral to it.

Separately, I'm trying to identify an abnormal bright lobulated heterogeneous mass that appears in multiple sagittal slices along the lateral abdominal wall, near structures I'm interpreting as liver, and it seems to correspond to a fluffy bright region also visible in axial 150.

The lateral lobulated mass with dark spots at axial 165 looks like bowel with gas, so the bright fluffy stuff is probably colon rather than a mass. I'm still uncertain about the anterior fluffy band though — it sits oddly close to the subcutaneous fat without a clear muscle layer separating it, and I'm trying to figure out if the oval homogeneous structure near the kidney at axial 150 could be liver, since that would show vessels.

Looking across slices now — axial 111 shows vessels consistent with liver, and I'm checking whether the oval at 150 connects to that structure, or whether it's actually a separate organ like the lower kidney pole, by comparing coronal 160 and sagittal 147/133 views.

content.text: axial 170/235 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 8/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm noticing a large region of intermediate-dark, homogeneous tissue anterior and left of the kidney/spine, extending from below the fluffy band down toward the bottom of the image. This could represent a sizable low-to-intermediate T2 mass, possibly a fibrous tumor like a desmoid or mesenteric mass, though it seems to intermix with bowel loops.

Reassessing the orientation: the spine's dark vertebral body and bright canal suggest anterior points to the image's right side rather than up, implying this may be a lateral decubitus position or a rotated image. This would mean the two kidney-like structures I'm seeing on opposite sides of the spine are actually both kidneys viewed from a different orientation than I assumed.

Working from that anterior-right orientation, the bright fluffy band at the image top likely corresponds to the patient's lateral/right flank, and the large homogeneous oval I noted earlier is probably the liver rather than another organ, consistent with the vessel pattern seen lower in the series. The dark, elongated anterior region could represent bowel loops or rectus muscle rather than a discrete mass.

I'm now wondering if the lobulated, heterogeneous bright structure with internal dark spots near the lateral-right area is actually the ascending colon or hepatic flexure containing stool, which would explain its irregular signal. That leaves the streaky, fluffy bright layer along the flank under the subcutaneous fat as the real question — normal abdominal wall muscles should appear darker, so this heterogeneous bright layer raises suspicion for something infiltrating the muscle, like a desmoid tumor of the abdominal wall.

I'm also noticing a large homogeneous intermediate-signal region centrally that spans multiple slices with dark linear streaks running through it — much bigger than a typical bowel loop and more consistent with a large fibrous mass like a mesenteric desmoid than normal bowel contents.

I'm getting confused about which axial orientation corresponds to coronal index 58 relative to the spine's posterior position — let me check coronal 76 directly with marks to clarify where that homogeneous region sits relative to the spine.

content.text: coronal 90/281 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 9/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm running low on time and trying to pin down the heterogeneous, fluffy tissue along the flank region seen across those axial slices, deciding whether I need more structured segmentation help or can just reason through the pattern directly.

Also I'm noticing a similar lobulated bright mass in the abdominal wall region on sagittal/coronal slices, considering whether it's desmoid-type fibromatosis versus fascial edema, and separately whether the round rim-and-dark-center structure near the liver is just the gallbladder or stomach rather than the tumor. Given the task points to a fibrous soft-tissue tumor, I'm leaning toward the abdominal wall mass as the target lesion and want to re-examine the axial 150 crop to confirm its boundaries.

Tracing the layers in axial 150 from skin inward, I see subcutaneous fat, then a fluffy bright band, then a thin dark curved band resembling muscle before reaching the liver — placing that fluffy band within the abdominal wall between fat and muscle, which fits a tumor infiltrating that layer, possibly with dark spots representing flow voids or fibrous septa continuing into axial 170.

I should pick the slice where the mass appears largest to begin segmentation, probably axial 150 since the fluffy band spans axial 129-184 and coronal 204-240 shows a sizable region there, so I'll check coronal 225 next.

This huge coronal extent spanning such a long curvilinear band makes me reconsider — it hugs the abdominal wall fascia like edema or omentum rather than a discrete mass, though it could also represent a large desmoid-type fibrous tumor. I'm not entirely settled on this interpretation yet.

Looking more closely at the fat-saturation quality, the subcutaneous fat appears grey-intermediate rather than fully suppressed, suggesting incomplete fat-sat with peripheral inhomogeneity. content.text:
I saved a mask for case F18, but I have low confidence that it covers the right structure.

**What was segmented:** a heterogeneous, T2-bright, streaky band lying deep to the subcutaneous fat and wrapping along the side and front of the abdominal wall. It looked to me like an infiltrative abdominal-wall mass, which fits a desmoid-type fibrous tumour. The final mask is one connected piece of 271.6 mL. It spans axial slices 99–218, coronal 93–254 and sagittal 46–221.

**Why confidence is low:**
- **Confusing orientation:** the scan is strongly oblique or rotated. In the axial images, anterior seems to be image-right rather than the labelled top, so I had to work out the anatomy from the spine and kidneys.
- **Unsure which structure is the tumour:** I decided the large smooth, uniform oval structure next to the right kidney is liver, because it has branching vessels in it. I did not confirm that, and if it is wrong, that oval is the more likely tumour and the mask is on the wrong structure.
- **Possible bowel included:** the lobulated part at the lateral end, with dark spots inside, may be colon containing gas or stool rather than tumour. It is partly inside the mask.
- **Extent:** my second point prompt nearly doubled the mask (151 → 275 mL), adding a long curved extension along the wall. I kept it, but it may include oedema or normal tissue. I removed 21 small stray pieces (3.3 mL in total).

**Candidates not accepted:**
- The large automatic proposals (roughly 50–420 mL) mostly traced fat or normal structures around the mask.
- A small 6.8 mL bright area near axial slice 86 may be a lower continuation of the lesion. I left it out.

I used 18 of 40 tool calls and 2 of 15 model prompts.
